title: Consolidation Module 1
description: The consolidation module that puts Module One (family roles, the generation gap) and Module Two (philanthropy) back on the table as thirteen tasks: the vocabulary of the household in context (members, within, household, responsibilities, assigned, expected, required, fulfil, arise, assistance, understanding, overburdened) and the arise / rise / raise family; the collocations that must be learnt whole (take out the rubbish, make decisions, maintain discipline, provide affection, take care of children, overcome a problem) and the of that take care keeps and look after refuses; word building read as a three-column table verb / noun / adjective (decide, grow, behave, expect, frustrate, satisfy, cooperate, volunteer, sacrifice), the cells English leaves empty because no verb exists on charity or philanthropy, the two facing adjectives of one verb (frustrating against frustrated), the irregular adverb good to well, and the -ing form of a verb used as the subject of a sentence; punctuation and capitalisation restored on a bare text (the full stop, the capital on a proper noun and on the adjective built on one, the comma after a long opening phrase, the apostrophe of possession) and the trap of capitalising an important common noun; rebuilding a paragraph from its scattered parts by their grammatical marks (a part opening on and or on an -ing form, a name given in full before every pronoun, a relative clause completing an earlier one); the present perfect against the simple past said with its reason, the for that does not choose the tense on its own, and the since clause that stays in the simple past; the four imposed rewrites of the module — wish plus a past for a present regret, otherwise turned into if plus a negative present with may, would rather plus a subject and a past when somebody else is to act, and allow plus to-infinitive turned into let plus the bare verb; the phrasal verbs of the consolidation (decide on, gaze at, turn out, pick up, look for, dream of, provide for, flow in, set off, catch up) with the separable ones and the pronoun that goes in the middle, and the difference between catch up and catch up with; the modals must, should, should have, shall and may, and need on both its faces — the full verb that takes to and do, and the modal needn't for the absence of necessity, with needn't have plus a past participle for what was done and was not necessary, against mustn't which forbids; the crossword clues that go from a definition, or from a word of the same family, to the word itself (overburdened, laughter, endow, comfort, pressure, donate, volunteer, affective, activism, charity); and the vocabulary of a biography with its passives and its superlative
